newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK court rejects legal attack on handover assembly.
newsitem.headline: HK court rejects legal attack on handover assembly.

text.p: Hong Kong's High Court on Thursday quashed a legal challenge by the popular Democratic Party against an unelected legislature that China plans to install after it takes over the British colony on July 1.
High Court judge Raymond Sears rejected an attempt to impose an injunction against the assembly and ruled that the judiciary should keep out of Britain and China's political squabbles.
Future Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa quickly applauded the ruling. A statement from Tung's office said he "welcomed the court could come to such a quick decision on the matter".

Hong Kong's democracy lobby, backed by Western states, has campaigned actively at home and overseas against the unelected chamber. Britain and the United States are pledged to boycott its inauguration at the handover ceremony.
The plaintiff, Democratic Party member Ng King-luen, 74, was represented in court by the party's leader, Martin Lee, one of the top barristers in the territory.

Lee, a party founder, was demanding a judicial ruling on whether the Provisional Legislature was usurping the lawmaking authority of the incumbent elected Legislative Council by processing new laws before the handover.
The party demanded a court injunction to halt bills passing through the interim partliament and a declaration that all bills passed before July 1 will be ruled void.
The case was based on an argument that Hong Kong's present constitution, known as the Letters Patent, allows only one legislature to pass laws for Hong Kong.

Sears said he could not issue a ruling on an assembly that meets outside Hong Kong. "I have no jurisdiction over a body which is meeting in China and passing what they called laws," Sears said in court.
So far, the 60-member shadow legislature has met across the border in the south China city of Shenzhen because of threats to challenge its legitimacy in Hong Kong.
Sears however indicated the courts would even allow it to meet on Hong Kong soil -- raising a prospect of two rival parliaments each passing laws up to June 30.
"I don't think they would be doing anything unlawful if they were to meet in Hong Kong...and they had decided to meet outside Hong Kong to prevent any political conflicts."
But he said any Hong Kong citizen could raise the matter again in the post-handover courts if they find a law passed by the body is unlawful after July 1.
Democratic Party vice-chairman and legislator Yeung Sum said the party might appeal against Sears' judgment. "We may go for appeal," he said.
"I'm disappointed, but not desperate. I will try to sue them again after July 1," Ng said.
The interim assembly till elections next year is packed with pro-China politicians and tycoons, chosen by a 400-strong China-controlled selection committee.

The Democratic Party emerged as Hong Kong's most popular in democratic elections held in 1995, when it gained 19 seats in the 60-seat Legislative Council, making it the biggest single political bloc in the chamber.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and British Prime Minister Tony Blair will boycott a swearing-in ceremony, scheduled for the early hours of July 1, although they will attend a midnight handover party shortly before that.
China arranged for the creation of the provisional legislature in retaliation for political reforms introduced by colonial Governor Chris Patten without China's consent.
The reforms enlarged the electoral franchise in the territory, which had previously enjoyed very little democracy.
